53_marg3902: The second book of the history of the Machabees, though it is shorter, yet in a certain way retraces the times of the earlier book of the same work, being more ancient in historical narration, except that the former makes at its beginning a brief mention of Alexander the Great of Macedon. For this book also recalls the benefits of King Seleucus, surnamed Nicanor, toward the Jews; the history of the Antiquities of Josephus and the Chronicle of Eusebius testify that he made the Jews worthy of their own commonwealth, and assigned them equal honour with the Macedonian and Greek inhabitants. Likewise Antiochus the Great, as the above-mentioned authorities testify, praises them in frequent letters and endows them with manifold gifts. The same book also has a narration different from the former, yet it does not destroy the truth of the history; for although it contains many testimonies of the former book, nevertheless it interposes many things which are not found in that. For it seems to have been written by those who stayed in the land, to those who were in foreign regions. Whence it begins thus.
53_marg3903: To the brethren that are throughout Egypt. This Demetrius, under whom the men of Jerusalem recall that they prayed for the Jews established in Egypt, is he who after Antiochus Eupator reigned over Asia and Syria, and who was himself surnamed Soter, that is, Saviour. For up to him the number of years that has been reckoned, that is, the hundred and sixty-ninth, runs. For Antiochus Epiphanes, who began to reign after the hundred and thirty-seventh year of the kingdom of the Greeks, reigned eleven years, Antiochus Eupator two years, and Demetrius Soter twelve years; these are, from the beginning of the reign of Seleucus Nicanor, king of Syria, from whom the times of the kingdom of the Greeks are reckoned, to the end of Demetrius, a hundred and sixty-two years. If to these are added the seven years of the reign of Alexander, who is described by Pompeius Trogus as ignoble and vicious and unworthy of royal dignity, but who nevertheless is said to have held the kingdom ten years, they make a hundred and sixty-nine. Let us say it another way. After Alexander, Antigonus first reigned over Asia, eighteen years, and after him Demetrius, who was also called Poliorcetes, reigned seventeen years. This Demetrius, then, in the seventeenth year of his reign gave himself up to Seleucus, and Asia was joined to the kingdom of Syria in the twenty-eighth year of Seleucus Nicanor. If, then, we begin now to reckon the series of years from the first year of the reign of Antigonus, who reigned in Asia seven years before Seleucus began to reign in Syria, placing those same seven years before the reign of Seleucus, and in that way bring the reckoning of the years of the kings of Syria down to the last year of Demetrius Soter, the whole sum of the former number is found there. But it is a wonder how in what follows Judas is said, in the hundred and eighty-eighth year, to have sent greeting with the senate to Aristobulus, the teacher of King Ptolemy, and to have sent word about the purification of the temple, which they were about to perform on the twenty-fifth day of the month Casleu, when Judas is read in the former book to have died long before the above-mentioned Demetrius. Indeed, in the sixth year of Demetrius, according to the credit of the chronicles, he is found to have been slain. But since the authors of those books themselves are uncertain, they seem not absurdly to differ in the reckoning of times, especially since in the books of the law the edition of the Seventy interpreters differs much from the Hebrew truth in the reckoning of years.
53_marg3904: We Jews, etc. But this Jason is the brother of the high priest Onias, whom the following part of this book shows to have flown to Antiochus Epiphanes, that is, a noble man who, out of ambition for the high priesthood, went to him and persuaded him to establish the Gentile rite at Jerusalem.
53_marg3905: Aristobulus was by birth a Jew, but is recognized as a Peripatetic philosopher, who wrote commentaries explaining Moses to Ptolemy Philometor, as the chronographers report, at the same time that Antiochus Epiphanes was reigning over Syria and Asia.
53_marg3906: From great dangers, etc. How Antiochus Epiphanes, who inflicted evils on the Jews beyond all the kings who were before him in Syria, lost his kingdom and ended his life, the former book of this history recounts, and Josephus testifies in the twelfth book of the Antiquities of the Jews, saying: King Antiochus, going through the upper province, heard of a city of the Persians excelling in riches, and in it a most precious temple of Diana, full of every kind of ornament; moreover he had heard that Alexander, son of Philip, king of the Macedonians, had left arms and breastplates there. Moved, therefore, he went out against Elymais and besieged it. But those who were in it, not at all terrified by his assault or by the siege, but resisting stubbornly, he departed almost deceived. For going out of the city they put him to flight and pursued him as far as Babylonia, where, when he had come after the loss of many of his soldiers, one of the Jews announced to him both the destruction of the generals whom he had left to fight against the Jews, and that the strength of the Jews had grown. Therefore, upon his former anxiety, this evil increasing, he fell into sickness, and while it lasted and the sufferings grew, he understood that he was to die. And calling together his friends he told them that his disease was grievous, confessing that he suffered these things because, afflicting the nation of the Jews, he had despoiled the temple and had despised God. When he had said this, he immediately expired. Whence I wonder at Polybius of Megalopolis, who, being a good man, says that Antiochus perished because he wished to lay waste the temple of Diana in Persia. For he who committed no sin at all, but only thought of it, is held to no guilt. But if it seems to Polybius that Antiochus ended his life for this reason, it is much more truly believed that the king perished on account of the sacrilege against the temple at Jerusalem.
53_marg3907: Indeed these things, which the Jews of Jerusalem write to the Jews who were throughout Egypt, about the fire found in the well, turned into the likeness of thick water, we have been able to find nowhere, neither in the writings or sayings of Esdras nor of Nehemias; just as that also which they affirm in what follows about the ark and the hiding of the tabernacle by Jeremias can in no way be found written in the book of Jeremias himself. Whence it is clear that they either learned these things by the tradition of their elders, or found them written in their apocryphal books. Let us therefore leave what is uncertain, and turn the pen to those things which are manifest by the sure attestation of the canonical books.
53_marg3908: Therefore when the holy city, etc. Therefore, because the high priests were various under various kings, we have judged it necessary, following the account of the historians, to recite the names of those priests who held the priesthood in the times of the kings, and also of those who were in the Jewish nation after the captivity of Babylon, that the truth of the history may appear the more clearly. First, then, Sadoch was priest of the temple which Solomon built. After him his son Achimaas succeeded to his honour. After him Joram, and after him Auxidramus. Then Nideas. After Nideas, Sudeas. After him Hylus. To Hylus succeeded Jonathan, and to him in turn Urias. To Urias, Nerias. After Nerias there was Odeas. After him Sellum. Then Elchias. After him Zara. And after him was Josedech, who was led captive into Babylon. All these, then, succeeded to the priesthood, sons after fathers, in order. After Josedech his son Jesus received the priesthood; under him the temple was rebuilt. And after him Joachim his son. When he also was dead, John his son received the honour. When John ended his life, his son Jaddus succeeded to the primacy of the priests; under him Alexander, king of Macedon, came to Jerusalem. After him Onias his son is held illustrious. After him Simon his son, whose surname was the Just, on account of his careful religion toward God and his ready kindness toward his citizens. Then Eleazar, brother of Simon, high priest of the Jews, took up the ministry of the temple, Simon’s son Onias being left very young. This Eleazar, at the request of Ptolemy Philadelphus, sent the seventy interpreters to interpret the divine law. After Eleazar his uncle Manasses received the priesthood. After Manasses Onias, son of Simon the Just, high priest of the Jews, is held illustrious; he, by not paying the customary tribute to king Ptolemy, drove him to anger. But Joseph, a man noble among his own, sent as ambassador by the Jews to Ptolemy, when he had deserved the king’s friendship by his many services to him, was made governor of Judea and of the neighbouring regions. After Onias, Simon, son of Onias, is held illustrious as high priest of the Jews. Under him Jesus the son of Sirach composed the book of Wisdom, which he called Panaretos, that is, capable of all virtues; and he made mention of Simon in it. After Simon his son Onias is held distinguished, to whom Arius king of the Lacedemonians sent ambassadors. He held the priesthood while Antiochus the Great reigned over Syria and Asia, and Seleucus Philopator his son, until Antiochus Epiphanes. Under this high priest Onias these things were done which are told of Simon, the overseer of the temple, while Seleucus Philopator reigned over Syria and Asia, to whom Antiochus Epiphanes succeeded in the kingdom. But Simon, overseer of the temple of Jerusalem, fleeing to Apollonius, the leader of Phenicia, and promising him many gifts, began to claim the priesthood for himself. When Seleucus heard this, he sent Heliodorus to look to the matter; who, when he had come into Judea, judging unjustly and doing many things wrongly, was frightened by divine signs against him, and returned to Seleucus. But the priest Onias had taken care that Simon should become a fugitive, etc. Finally, this history, according to the rule of tropology, hints that all who, urged on by pride and avarice, presume to defile the sanctification of the Lord and to handle it unworthily with polluted hands, are to be punished by heavenly judgment; for, as the truth attests, the house of God is a house of prayer for all nations, nor is it lawful for anyone to make it a den of thieves. Hence the Psalmist also says: “Holiness becometh thy house, O Lord, unto length of days.” Nor is it lawful to do or store anything there, except to be free for the praises and prayers of God alone. Whence the Lord himself in the Gospel cast out of the temple those who sold and bought in it, and poured out the money of the moneychangers, and overthrew the chairs of them that sold doves. And after this was done he was daily teaching in the temple. According to allegory, however, Onias, the great priest of God and keeper of the figurative temple, signifies the Lord the Saviour, who was made by God the Father a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchisedech, and is keeper and inhabitant of the temple of the true God, which is the Church; which the name of Onias seems sufficiently to express. For Onias is interpreted the sorrow of the Lord, or the Lord of sorrow; and who can be better called the sorrowing Lord than our redeemer, of whom it is said through Isaias: “We have seen him, and there was no sightliness, that we should be desirous of him: despised, and the most abject of men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with infirmity. Surely he hath borne our infirmities and carried our sorrows.” Heliodorus, however, the invader or plunderer of the treasury of the Lord, signifies pagans, or Jews, or even heretics, who without reverence for God wish to abuse his gifts and turn them to a wicked act. For pagans invade the treasure of the temple of God when they strive to destroy the faith and worship of Christ. The Jews invade when they desire to confound the Christian religion with the ceremonies of the old law. Heretics also invade when they long to corrupt the truth of the gospel and the sincerity of the law of God with false doctrines. But when Onias prayed, there came down a terrible horseman, having golden armour: he, namely, of whom John wrote in his Apocalypse, saying: “I saw heaven opened, and behold a white horse; and he that sat upon him was called faithful and true, and with justice doth he judge. And his eyes were as a flame of fire, and on his head were many diadems, and he had a name written, which no man knoweth but himself. And he was clothed with a garment sprinkled with blood; and his name is called the Word of God.” To the members of Christ who pray, he himself brings help, “who is the way, the truth, and the life”; both to overcome enemies and to terrify the presumptions of the wicked: his horse was white, because his Nativity was incorrupt; and his garment bloody, because the death of his flesh was innocent; and he himself terrible, because exceedingly wonderful, and a most just judge. He was adorned with the best coverings, because he shines most brightly with the beauty of all virtues; his armour was golden, because his works are wonderful. For by his gift his Church has “the shield of faith,” the breastplate of justice, “the helmet of salvation, the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God.” With these arms he himself daily fights in his members against his enemies. This horseman, namely, with violence struck Heliodorus with his front hooves, because the sacrament of the incarnation overthrows all enemies, that is, pagans, Jews, and heretics, so that, confounded, they may at some time desist from the savagery of their crimes.
53_marg3909: Those two young men, then, who appeared with the horseman himself, “beautiful and strong, bright and glorious, and in comely apparel, who stood by Onias on either side, and scourged Heliodorus without ceasing with many stripes,” signify the teachers of both testaments, who, standing around the incarnation of Christ, comely in the strength of faith and good works, best in the glory of miracles, and most beautiful in the apparel of holy knowledge and wisdom, existing at various times, scourge by their preachings the insensibility of the wicked, and compel them to fall to the ground. And so it will come about that he who proudly attacked before the temple appears powerless by the correction of discipline, “for there is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord,” because “whatsoever the Lord hath pleased he hath done, in heaven, in earth, in the sea, and in all the deeps,” and there is none who can resist his will; he is the Lord of all. But that Onias, offering a saving victim for the man’s health, saved Heliodorus himself, wrapped round with great darkness, signifies that the mercy of our Redeemer often confers the benefit of conversion on the ungrateful and undeserving, so that by the grace of him who offered himself a saving victim for the sins of the world they may be rescued from their errors, and willingly, from the power of Satan, in whose wickedness they were once captives, they may according to his will give thanks to their Redeemer, and proclaim his praise in all the earth.
53_marg3910: But after Seleucus, etc. Of this Josephus relates thus. About the same time, Onias the chief of the priests having died, Antiochus conferred the chief priesthood on his brother. For the son whom Onias had left was still an infant. But we shall show in its proper place the particulars which seem to belong to this boy. But from Jesus, for he was the brother of Onias, the king in anger took away the chief priesthood, and gave it to his younger brother, named Onias. For Simon had these three sons, to whom the chief priesthood, as we said before, came. And Jesus indeed named himself Jason, but Onias was named Menelaus. Therefore Jesus, the chief of the priests, first stirred up sedition against Menelaus, and the multitude of the people being divided into two, they stood on the side of Menelaus the son of Tobias, but the greater part of the people helped Jason. Whence Menelaus and the sons of Thobias, in distress, went away to Antiochus, making known to him that they wished to abandon the laws of their fathers and their way of life, and to observe the customs of the Greeks. They asked him therefore to permit them to build a gymnasium at Jerusalem. And when he had granted it, they concealed their circumcision, so that in nakedness they might not appear unlike the Greeks. And leaving all the other things which their ancestral custom imposed on them, they followed the deeds and rites of other nations. So far Josephus.
53_marg3911: But I wonder how, Onias being dead, Antiochus is said to have given the priesthood to the brother of Jason, since this History does not agree with this narration, as will be shown in what follows. Finally, Antiochus Epiphanes, when he had withdrawn by order of the senate from the region of the Ptolemies, which he had suddenly invaded, came to Judea, and there handed over the pontificate to Jesus, who is also Jason, the brother of Onias; and when he had afterwards been expelled, he gave him as successor Onias, surnamed Menelaus. And so, sedition having arisen among the chiefs on account of the dignity of the priesthood, the seeds of great miseries sprang up. This faction, then, of the proud and of transgressors of the law of God brings us no allegory useful for edification. But, alas, in this time Jason has found many imitators of his crime: those who are set forth in the Church of the people of God, and by the blood of his only-begotten Son the Redeemer, having abandoned the teaching of the Gospel and true religion, fly from the worship of the one God, which is commended and made known there, to secret idolatry by depraved morals; while through ambition for money and the riches of the present life, leading a luxurious life, detestable to God, and heeding the favour of flatterers, they draw many with them to perdition. These indeed, according to the Apostle, “profess that they know God, but in their works they deny him.” For they are not content with moderate food and clothing. But “they that will become rich, fall into temptation, and into the snare of the devil, and into many unprofitable and hurtful desires, which drown men into destruction and perdition. For the desire of money is the root of all evils; which some coveting have erred from the faith, and have entangled themselves in many sorrows.”
53_marg3912: Now when the game that was used every fifth year, etc. While Ozias, who is also Azarias, the leprous king, reigned in Judea, and Phacea in Jerusalem, and Eschylus among the Athenians, and Aemulius among the Latins, in the second year of Eschylus, judge of the Athenians, the first Olympiad was held, in which Choreb of Elis was victor. The men of Elis hold the contest every fifth year, four years having been completed in between, in which four yearly rulers are appointed; this Olympiad Iphitus, son of Praxonides, or of Aemon, first instituted. From this time the Greek history of times is believed true; for before this they brought forth differing opinions, as each one thought good. For it is described that Antiochus then celebrated this game of the fifth year at Tyre, and the things that are afterwards recorded of Jason and Menelaus were done later. Jason indeed had taken captive his own brother, that is, Onias the elder, son of Simon. By Menelaus, that is, the younger Onias, who had two names, he was accused before the king, and deceived, and driven out a fugitive into the country of the Ammonites. Menelaus however obtained the principality, but did nothing about the money promised to the king for the priesthood; for which cause he too was likewise removed from the priesthood, Lysimachus succeeding him. While he held the priesthood, Menelaus, Antiochus being absent, thinking he had got a convenient time on account of quelling the Tarsians and Mallotes, stole certain vessels of gold from the temple and gave them to Andronicus the officer, whom the king had left to guard the region. Whence Onias the elder, his brother, whom Jason had taken captive, moved, rebuked Menelaus for the impiety committed, keeping himself in a safe place at Antioch beside Daphne. Whence Menelaus, going to Andronicus, asked him to kill Onias. And when he had come to Onias, and given his right hand with an oath, although Onias was suspicious of him, and had persuaded him to come forth from the sanctuary, he at once slew him, not fearing justice; for which cause not only the Jews but other nations also were indignant, and took it grievously, at the unjust death of so great a man. Hence the Jews likewise, and the Greeks, went to the king when he returned from the places of Cilicia, revealing what had been done. Antiochus, moved by this even to the shedding of tears, remembering the sobriety and modesty of the dead man, and inflamed in mind, ordered Andronicus, stripped of his purple, to be led about through the whole city, and in the same place where he had committed the impiety against Onias, the sacrilegious man to be deprived of life, the Lord repaying him a fitting punishment. For many sacrileges having been committed in the temple by Lysimachus at the counsel of Menelaus, and the rumour spread abroad, a multitude was gathered against Lysimachus. Some seized stones, others strong clubs, and some threw ashes at Lysimachus; and many indeed were wounded, some also struck down, and all were turned to flight; and the sacrilegious man himself they killed beside the treasury. Concerning these things, therefore, judgment began to be agitated against Menelaus. And when the king had come to Tyre, three men sent by the elders brought the matter before him. And when Menelaus was being overcome, he promised Ptolemy much money to persuade the king. And so Ptolemy, going to the king, who was placed in a certain court as if to take the air, brought him off his opinion; and Menelaus, guilty of all malice, he acquitted of the charges, but the wretched men, who even if they had pleaded their cause before the Scythians would have been judged innocent, he condemned to death.
53_marg3913: Portents, therefore, sometimes portend prosperity, and sometimes prefigure adversity; but always according to what the supreme judge decides is fitting for each thing and time. Nor is it a wonder that in the times of the Machabees horsemen in golden robes, and cohorts armed with spears, were seen running through the air, and the gleaming splendour of golden arms foretold adversity to come and a disaster about to fall on the Jews; since before the overthrow of Jerusalem, under Vespasian and Titus, as Josephus testifies, we have learned that a star shining like a sword in every respect hung over the city from above, and moreover a comet burning with deadly flames was seen throughout the whole year. But before the time of the destruction and of the war, when the people were gathering for the feast of unleavened bread, on the eighth day of the month Antiochus, which is April, at the ninth hour of the night, so great a brightness of light surrounded the altar and the temple that all thought it had become the brightest day; and it lasted for half an hour. This seemed favourable to the unskilled and ignorant; but the deadly portent did not escape those learned in the law and all the upright teachers. At the same feast also a heifer, brought to the sacrifices and standing at the altars, gave birth to a lamb in the very hands of the ministers. Moreover the door of the inner temple, which faced east, though it was covered with bronze as usual, and so of immense weight that it was scarcely closed by twenty men pushing with utmost effort, and was held fast, secured with iron bars and bolts and with bars sunk deep, suddenly at the sixth hour of the night appeared opened of its own accord. Moreover, when the feast day had passed, some days after, on the twenty-first day of the month Artemisius, which is called May among us, a prodigious sight appeared, almost beyond belief, which would truly have been thought false, had not the destruction that followed their evils confirmed the faith of hidden things. For near sunset chariots and four-horse teams were seen carried through the air over the whole region, and cohorts of armed men mingling with the clouds, and cities encircled by unexpected armies. Likewise on another feast day, which is called Pentecost, when the priests entered the temple by night to fulfil the ministries as usual, they first perceived certain movements and noises, then heard voices beneath them saying: Let us depart hence. Another still more terrible thing is added. For a certain Jesus, son of Ananias, a plebeian and a rustic, four years before the war, when the city was still in peace and abundance, at the feast of tabernacles suddenly began to cry out: A voice from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four winds, a voice over Jerusalem and over the temple, a voice over bridegrooms and over brides, a voice over the people. And ceaselessly, day and night, going about through all the streets, he cried this, until some of the chief men of the people, moved with indignation as at an ill omen, seized the man and afflicted him with many blows. But he, saying nothing at all for himself, and not even entreating those who stood about, repeated the same words with equal obstinacy and cry. Then the princes, understanding, as was the case, that there was something more than human in the man, brought him to the Roman judge, before whom, torn with scourges to the very bones, he shed neither prayers nor tears; but uttering the same voice piteously and with a kind of wailing, he pronounced it at nearly every word, adding also this: Woe, woe to Jerusalem. The wretched city therefore endured all these prodigies because always, according to the testimony of the lawgiver, it acted in sedition against the Lord, and, ungrateful for his benefits, treated insultingly and killed the servants of the supreme father of the family who were sent to it by him. And last of all, killing the heir himself, they cast him out of the camp. Whence the Lord himself in the Gospel, rebuking the unbelieving city, says: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered together thy children, as the hen doth gather her chickens under her wings, and thou wouldest not? Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate.” For this was foretold of old, and this was fulfilled in later times, that the most savage murderers should receive the fitting reward of their guilt, so that some were killed by famine, some slain, and the captives were led by the enemies into all parts of the world. And so was fulfilled that word of Jeremias, who prophesied of the same nation and city, saying: “Juda hath removed her dwelling place because of her affliction, and the greatness of her bondage: she hath dwelt among the nations, and she hath found no rest: all her persecutors have taken her in the midst of straits. The ways of Sion mourn, because there are none that come to the solemn feast: all her gates are broken down: her priests sigh: her virgins are in affliction, and she is oppressed with bitterness.”
